title: What I learned making a ninja card battler with AI art and AI-written code (free, plays in the browser)
author: im_siahhh
selftext:
Mon-Fri I’m a chemist helping with oil research, not a programmer or an artist, and I've spent the last month making The Thirteenth Seal, a ninja card battler where both players lock in a card and reveal at the same time. It's out on itch.io now with a five-act story, a roguelike mode and online play, so I wanted to share what the AI side actually looked like.

The character art and comic panels came from Google Flow, and the music from SUNO. The hardest part by far was consistency. Six heroes appear across 23 fighter portraits, 351 cards and every story panel, and the model kept drifting on small details like hair, outfits and which hand someone holds a weapon in. On some occasions characters even had extra limbs haha. What worked best was writing a fixed description for each character and pasting it into every prompt word for word instead of paraphrasing. This alongside a reference image, usually, did the trick, but even then it slips: my original title art had a seventh character that doesn't exist in the game, and I didn't notice until after launch. Now I count heads on every group image.

All the code, the text and the story dialogue were written with Claude. I designed the rules, the story and the characters, then described what I wanted and reviewed what came back, stringently. The whole game is one HTML file. The thing that made it workable was having Claude test its own changes by running the game in a headless browser, including bots playing full online matches against each other, rather than me clicking through everything by hand after each change.

The part I'm proudest of is online play without a game server. Both players' browsers run the same match from a shared random seed, and Firebase only passes moves between them. Your card stays hidden until both of you have locked in, both screens compare a checksum every turn, and Ranked results from the two players are checked against each other. Reported matches can be replayed move by move. It all runs on Firebase's free plan.

Where AI struggled: game balance.   
Coming from a competitive Yugioh and Pokemon background, I can come up with card/ability ideas in seconds. Claude can write them in minutes, but it can't tell you whether that card breaks the game. That still takes playing it, whether it be myself or other real players helping.

It's free with no ads or real-money purchases: https://siahmadethis.itch.io/the-thirteenth-seal

Curious how others handle character consistency across hundreds of images. Do you lock a reference sheet, use image-to-image, or something else?
